description: Maps serialized-data indicators to the programming language, runtime and format they originate from.

indicators: Raw stream header AC ED 00 05
Base64 prefix rO0AB
Base64 prefix H4sI when the stream is gzip-wrapped
signatures.details: Binary stream produced by ObjectOutputStream and consumed by ObjectInputStream. It encodes class names and field values, so the receiving JVM instantiates classes chosen by the sender while reading the stream.
signatures.risk: Deserializing untrusted streams can trigger gadget chains present on the classpath, leading to remote code execution, denial of service or arbitrary file access.
signatures.remediation: Do not deserialize untrusted input natively. Use a data-only format, or enforce a class allow-list with ObjectInputFilter (JEP 290).

indicators: XML root element <java version="...">
XML elements such as <object class="java.*">
signatures.details: XML document in the java.beans.XMLDecoder format. The decoder constructs arbitrary objects and invokes the constructors and methods described by the XML elements.
signatures.risk: Attacker-controlled XML can instantiate arbitrary classes and call arbitrary methods, which commonly results in remote code execution.
signatures.remediation: Replace XMLDecoder with a binding library that maps to fixed types, and reject documents that use the java.beans format.

indicators: Raw header 00 01 00 00 00 FF FF FF FF
Base64 prefix AAEAAAD/////
signatures.details: Binary payload produced by BinaryFormatter. It embeds assembly-qualified type names that the formatter resolves and instantiates while reading.
signatures.risk: Microsoft documents BinaryFormatter as insecure for untrusted data; a crafted payload can lead to remote code execution.
signatures.remediation: Migrate to a type-safe serializer such as System.Text.Json or DataContractSerializer with known types. BinaryFormatter is obsolete and unsupported in modern .NET.

indicators: Hidden form field __VIEWSTATE
Base64 prefix /wE when the state is not encrypted
signatures.details: Serialized page and control state that ASP.NET Web Forms round-trips through the client. Its integrity depends on ViewState MAC and the machineKey; a predictable or leaked key allows forged state to be deserialized by the server.
signatures.risk: With a known or weak machineKey, or with MAC disabled, forged ViewState can lead to deserialization of attacker-chosen objects.
signatures.remediation: Keep ViewState MAC and encryption enabled, use a unique random machineKey per application, and keep the key out of source control.

indicators: Raw header 80 02 through 80 05 with trailing byte 2E
Base64 prefixes gAJ, gAN, gAS, gAV
signatures.details: Opcode stream produced by pickle.dumps. The unpickler can import modules and call arbitrary callables through __reduce__, so loading a pickle is equivalent to running code supplied by its author.
frameworks: Cache and session backends configured with pickle
Task queues configured with a pickle serializer
signatures.risk: Unpickling untrusted data results in arbitrary code execution.
signatures.remediation: Never unpickle untrusted data. Use JSON or another data-only format, and authenticate any pickle that must cross a trust boundary with an HMAC.

indicators: Raw header 04 08
Base64 prefix BAh
signatures.details: Binary format produced by Marshal.dump. Marshal.load can instantiate arbitrary classes and trigger methods on them while loading.
signatures.risk: Loading attacker-controlled Marshal data can lead to remote code execution through gadget chains in loaded gems.
signatures.remediation: Use JSON for sessions, cookies and caches, keep secret_key_base private, and never call Marshal.load on untrusted input.

indicators: Text prefix O:<length>:"<ClassName>":<count>:{
URL-encoded or Base64-wrapped variants of the same prefix
signatures.details: Text format produced by serialize(). Object entries name the class and its properties; unserialize() instantiates the class and runs magic methods such as __wakeup and __destruct, which enables property-oriented programming.
frameworks: Composer-loaded libraries that provide gadget classes
signatures.risk: Untrusted input reaching unserialize() can lead to object injection, file operations or remote code execution depending on available classes.
signatures.remediation: Use json_encode and json_decode. If unserialize() is unavoidable, pass allowed_classes => false and sign the data with an HMAC.

indicators: Text prefix a:<count>:{
signatures.details: Text array produced by serialize(). An array alone carries no class names, but the same unserialize() sink normally accepts nested objects, so the endpoint may be exploitable with object payloads.
signatures.risk: Confirms that the application round-trips serialized PHP data through the client and passes it to unserialize().
signatures.remediation: Replace serialize and unserialize with JSON for client-visible state, and sign any state that must be stored client-side.

indicators: Marker _$$ND_FUNC$$_ inside a JSON string value
signatures.details: The node-serialize package encodes functions as strings behind this marker and rebuilds them by evaluating the string when unserialize() runs, so function bodies sent by a client can execute on the server.
signatures.risk: Untrusted input passed to unserialize() can lead to remote code execution inside the Node.js process.
signatures.remediation: Remove node-serialize, exchange plain JSON data only, and never revive functions from client-supplied input.

indicators: JSON property "$type" holding a .NET type name
signatures.details: Json.NET writes $type with an assembly-qualified type name when TypeNameHandling is enabled. If the server honors client-supplied type names, the sender chooses which type is instantiated.
signatures.risk: Unsafe TypeNameHandling lets attackers instantiate arbitrary types, which can lead to remote code execution through gadget types.
signatures.remediation: Use TypeNameHandling.None, or restrict allowed types with a custom ISerializationBinder allow-list.

indicators: JSON property "__type" holding a .NET type name
signatures.details: JavaScriptSerializer with a type resolver and DataContractJsonSerializer emit __type to describe the concrete type. Servers that resolve this value on input let the sender influence the instantiated type.
signatures.risk: Unrestricted type resolution can allow instantiation of unintended types during deserialization.
signatures.remediation: Do not use SimpleTypeResolver on untrusted input, and limit deserialization to an explicit list of known types.

indicators: JSON property "@type" holding a dotted class name
signatures.details: Fastjson autoType and Jackson type information use @type to name the class to instantiate. A dotted package-style class name strongly suggests a JVM backend.
signatures.risk: If the library honors client-supplied class names, attackers can select which class is instantiated and reach gadget classes.
signatures.remediation: Disable autoType and default typing, or enforce an allow-list of permitted classes or a PolymorphicTypeValidator.

indicators: JSON property "@class" holding a dotted class name
signatures.details: Jackson uses @class as the default property for JsonTypeInfo with Id.CLASS and for default typing. The value is a fully qualified Java class name that the mapper loads and instantiates.
signatures.risk: Unrestricted polymorphic typing allows attacker-selected classes to be instantiated during deserialization.
signatures.remediation: Avoid Id.CLASS and default typing for untrusted input, and configure a restrictive PolymorphicTypeValidator.

indicators: JSON property "javaClass" holding a dotted class name
signatures.details: The javaClass hint is used by jabsorb and similar JSON-RPC bridges to carry the fully qualified Java class of a value, which the server resolves while unmarshalling.
signatures.risk: Client-controlled class names can lead to instantiation of unintended classes during unmarshalling.
signatures.remediation: Retire the legacy bridge or restrict unmarshalling to an explicit set of expected classes.

indicators: JSON property "_class" holding a dotted class name
signatures.details: Spring Data stores the persisted Java type name in _class so documents can be mapped back to the right class. Data that round-trips through the client may let the sender influence the mapped type.
signatures.risk: Exposes backend class names and may allow type confusion if the hint is honored on input.
signatures.remediation: Do not accept raw persisted documents from clients, and map input onto fixed DTO classes.

indicators: JSON property "$class" or "class" holding a dotted type name
signatures.details: A generic type hint key that several ecosystems use. The backend language cannot be inferred from the key alone; dotted lowercase package names usually indicate Java, while names followed by an assembly name indicate .NET.
signatures.risk: If the server resolves the supplied name, the sender may control which type is instantiated.
signatures.remediation: Do not resolve client-supplied type names; bind input to fixed types.
